title: Policy Administration Systems (PAS) for Life Insurance

questions.stem: A Policy Administration System (PAS) is best described as:

opts.x: The software system used by insurance brokers to generate client quotations and manage broker commission claims.
The core software system that creates, stores, and manages all insurance policy records across the policy lifecycle, from application to termination.
The actuarial modelling platform used by the Statutory Actuary to calculate life insurance reserves.
The financial accounting system that records premium income and claims payments for NAICOM statutory financial returns.

questions.answer: (B) The core software system that creates, stores, and manages all insurance policy records across the policy lifecycle, from application to termination.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The PAS is the system of record for all insurance policies — it is the primary operational database of the life insurer. Every policy that exists is created in the PAS; every premium payment is recorded in the PAS; every claims payment instruction originates from the PAS; every regulatory report is generated from the PAS. Without the PAS, the insurer has no authoritative record of its obligations to policyholders. It is the foundational technology layer on which all other systems depend.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) A broker quotation system is a separate technology (often a CRM or standalone quoting tool) used by intermediaries — not the insurer's PAS.
(C) The actuarial modelling platform (Prophet, Moses) is a separate analytical tool — the PAS provides the data input, but actuarial modelling is done in a different system.
(D) The financial accounting system (ERP, general ledger) records financial transactions — the PAS generates the source data that feeds into accounting, but the two are distinct systems.

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, a life insurer's PAS claims module must automatically track which statutory timelines?

opts.x: A 10-day acknowledgement target and a 90-day settlement target.
A 5-day acknowledgement target and a 60-day settlement target from notification of the claim.
A 24-hour acknowledgement target and a 14-day settlement target.
A 7-day acknowledgement target and a 45-day settlement target.

questions.answer: (B) A 5-day acknowledgement target and a 60-day settlement target from notification of the claim.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Under NIIRA 2025 (s.210) a valid claim must be settled within 60 days of notification, and the book recommends a 5-business-day written acknowledgement of each claim notification as an internal service standard (no statutory acknowledgement period has been confirmed). The PAS claims module must track both deadlines, alert when a claim nears the acknowledgement deadline without confirmation, and escalate as a claim approaches or breaches the 60-day settlement deadline.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) A 10-day acknowledgement and 90-day settlement exceed both limits.
(C) 24 hours and 14 days are admirable internal targets but are not the statutory standard the module must enforce.
(D) A 7-day acknowledgement exceeds the recommended 5-business-day standard; a 45-day settlement is inside the statutory maximum but is not the statutory standard.

questions.stem: The NDPA 2023 data localisation requirement means a Nigerian life insurer deploying a cloud-based PAS must ensure that:

opts.x: All policyholder data is stored exclusively on servers owned by the insurer itself.
Policyholder data is encrypted at all times and backed up to at least three separate geographic locations.
The primary storage of Nigerian policyholder personal data is on servers physically located in Nigeria.
Policyholder data may only be accessed by staff who are physically present in Nigeria.

questions.answer: (C) The primary storage of Nigerian policyholder personal data is on servers physically located in Nigeria.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

NDPA 2023 (and the GAID 2025 implementation directive) requires data controllers to store and process Nigerian citizens' personal data on servers physically located within Nigeria as the primary data store. This data localisation requirement means that a cloud-based PAS must be deployed on Nigerian-domiciled cloud infrastructure (either an AWS Nigeria region, Azure Nigeria region, or a Nigerian data centre) — not on servers in the US, Europe, or Asia, even if these are offered by major cloud providers. Cross-border data transfers to foreign servers are permitted for specific backup or processing purposes but require specific safeguards.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) The insurer does not need to own the servers — it can use cloud infrastructure that is physically located in Nigeria. Ownership is not the criterion; physical location is.
(B) Encryption and geographic backup are security best practices but do not satisfy the localisation requirement — data encrypted in a London data centre is still not localised in Nigeria.
(D) Staff access is an access control matter — the localisation requirement is about where data is stored, not where it is accessed from.

questions.stem: The daily premium reconciliation report from a life insurance PAS is primarily used to:

opts.x: Calculate the reinsurance cession due to treaty reinsurers for the month.
Match expected premium income from the billing schedule against actual bank receipts, identifying unmatched items for investigation.
Calculate the surrender values payable on policies presented for cancellation during the period.
Verify that agent commission has been paid at the correct NAICOM-approved rate for each policy.

questions.answer: (B) Match expected premium income from the billing schedule against actual bank receipts, identifying unmatched items for investigation.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The daily premium reconciliation is a financial control process: the PAS generates a billing schedule (all premiums due on that day's anniversary policies); the bank provides a payment file (all receipts credited to the insurer's premium collection accounts that day); and the reconciliation matches the two files. Unmatched items — premiums expected but not received, or receipts that cannot be matched to a specific policy — require investigation. Without daily reconciliation, the insurer cannot accurately track which policies are in force (premiums received) and which are in grace period or lapsed (premiums not received).
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Reinsurance cession calculations are a monthly treaty reporting function — not the purpose of the daily premium reconciliation.
(C) Surrender value calculations are triggered by specific policyholder requests — not produced as part of a daily reconciliation.
(D) Commission verification against NAICOM rates is a compliance function performed on policy issuance — not the daily reconciliation's purpose.

questions.stem: The primary risk of skipping the parallel run phase during a PAS implementation is:

opts.x: The insurer's NAICOM licence may be suspended during the implementation period.
Data discrepancies between the old and new system, which would have been identified during a parallel run, may only be discovered after the old system has been decommissioned.
Agent commission payments cannot be made during the implementation period.
The new PAS vendor may terminate the implementation contract if the parallel run is not completed.

questions.answer: (B) Data discrepancies between the old and new system, which would have been identified and resolved during the parallel run, may only be discovered after the old system has been decommissioned.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

A parallel run involves operating both the old and new PAS simultaneously for a defined period (typically 3–6 months), processing all real transactions through both systems and comparing outputs. Differences in policy records, premium calculations, reserve computations, or claims data are identified and resolved while the old system is still available as a reference. Skipping the parallel run and going live directly on the new system means that any data discrepancies — migrated incorrectly, miscalculated by the new system, or simply incompletely transferred — are only discovered when they cause operational failures (a policyholder's coverage is incorrectly terminated; a claim is incorrectly declined; a premium is not correctly applied). At that point, the old system's data may no longer be accessible for comparison.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) NAICOM does not automatically suspend licences during PAS implementations — the insurer must maintain compliance throughout, but the parallel run is not itself a NAICOM requirement.
(C) Commission payments must be maintained during implementation — this is an operational requirement managed through the transition plan, not a specific consequence of skipping the parallel run.
(D) Vendor contract termination provisions are a commercial matter and would not typically be triggered by skipping a parallel run phase.

questions.stem:
A mid-size Nigerian life insurer with 85,000 in-force policies is evaluating whether to replace its 12-year-old legacy PAS. The current system: produces NAICOM quarterly returns only after 3 days of manual data extraction; has no API connectivity; cannot produce IFRS 17-compliant cohort data without a separate data warehouse; and is no longer actively supported by its vendor.
(a) Using the PAS Assessment Framework from Chapter 29, evaluate the urgency of the case for PAS replacement.
(b) Describe the five key selection criteria the insurer should use to evaluate replacement platforms, explaining the specific Nigerian regulatory requirements that each criterion must satisfy.
(c) Explain the data migration risk that the insurer faces and describe the approach to data validation that should be completed before go-live.
(d) Explain how the insurer should maintain NAICOM regulatory compliance and NIIRA 2025 claims SLA compliance during the PAS transition period.

model.h: Part (a) — PAS Assessment Framework: Urgency Evaluation

rows: Assessment Dimension
Current System Score and Urgency Implication
Regulatory compliance capability

CRITICAL FAILURE. Cannot produce NAICOM quarterly returns without 3 days of manual extraction — this creates timing risk for regulatory filing deadlines and opens the insurer to regulatory sanction if returns are ever filed late due to extraction failures. Cannot produce IFRS 17-compliant cohort data — a mandatory financial reporting requirement from the IFRS 17 adoption date.
API connectivity

CRITICAL FAILURE. No API connectivity means the insurer cannot participate in any embedded insurance partnership, cannot connect to bancassurance partner systems in real time, and cannot integrate with digital distribution channels. This is not merely a future capability gap — it is the reason the insurer cannot grow its digital premium income today.
Vendor support status

HIGH URGENCY. An unsupported PAS has no security patches, no bug fixes, and no feature updates. The insurer is running production insurance operations on software that its own vendor will not maintain — creating escalating operational risk with every passing month.
Operational efficiency

HIGH URGENCY. 3 days of manual data extraction for NAICOM returns represents significant staff time and introduces data integrity risk from manual intervention. This inefficiency compounds as the in-force book grows.

model.h: Overall assessment: The case for PAS replacement is URGENT. Three of four assessment dimensions are at critical or high failure levels. This is not a technology decision that can be deferred for budget reasons — the regulatory compliance gaps (NAICOM return production; IFRS 17 cohort data) create direct regulatory risk that the Board and Statutory Actuary cannot continue to manage through workarounds.
Part (b) — Five Key Selection Criteria

rows: Criterion
Nigerian Regulatory Requirement It Must Satisfy
1. Real-time NAICOM regulatory reporting

Must produce all required NAICOM quarterly returns (premiums, claims, reserves, solvency ratio, investment data) directly from the PAS without manual extraction — and must be updateable when NAICOM changes return formats.
2. IFRS 17 cohort data capability

Must be able to segment in-force policies by product type, annual cohort, and risk group — and produce the expected cash flow, risk adjustment, and CSM inputs required for IFRS 17 GMM and VFA calculations without a separate data warehouse.
3. API-first architecture

Must provide documented REST APIs for: policy issuance (for embedded insurance partners); premium collection (for digital payment providers); claims notification (for corporate agents and partners); and policy status enquiry (for self-service portals and agent apps).
4. NDPA 2023 data localisation compliance

Must be deployable on Nigeria-domiciled cloud infrastructure (or on-premise in Nigeria) with no requirement for primary data storage on servers outside Nigeria. Must include data access logging (for NDPA 2023 audit trail requirements for special category data access).
5. NIIRA 2025 claims SLA tracking

Must include a claims workflow module that: automatically timestamps every claim notification; tracks the 5-day acknowledgement deadline; tracks the 60-day settlement deadline from the notification date; generates escalation alerts for approaching deadlines; and produces the claims settlement performance report required by NAICOM.

model.h: Part (c) — Data Migration Risk and Validation Approach

The primary data migration risk is the loss of data integrity when migrating 85,000 policy records from a 12-year-old legacy system to the new PAS. Specific risks: incomplete migration (records exist in the old system but do not appear in the new); data transformation errors (dates, currency formats, policy status codes converted incorrectly); truncation (long text fields cut short in the new system's schema).

Validation approach before go-live:
1. Pre-migration data audit: Extract and profile the full legacy PAS dataset before migration. Identify: duplicate policy records; incomplete records (missing mandatory fields); legacy codes that do not map cleanly to the new system's schema. Cleanse before migrating.
2. Sample validation: After migration, randomly sample 5% of migrated policy records across all product types and vintage years. Verify each sampled record against the corresponding legacy record — confirming all fields are correctly migrated.
3. Financial reconciliation: Reconcile the total in-force premium income, reserve values, and claims liabilities produced by the new PAS against the equivalent figures from the legacy system and the most recent NAICOM statutory return. Any material discrepancy must be investigated and resolved before go-live.
4. Claims history verification: Verify that claims history for in-force policies is correctly migrated — including outstanding claims, previously declined claims (for moratorium enforcement), and paid claims.
Part (d) — Maintaining Compliance During Transition

NAICOM regulatory compliance during transition:
1. Run the legacy system in parallel for the first 3 months post-new PAS launch — producing NAICOM returns from both systems and reconciling the outputs. Use the legacy system as the authoritative source for regulatory reporting during the parallel period until the new system's outputs are validated.
2. Notify NAICOM of the PAS migration project before go-live — providing the project timeline and the parallel run plan. This creates regulatory transparency and provides advance notice if any delay requires a timeline extension for returns.

NIIRA 2025 claims SLA compliance during transition:
1. Designate a claims continuity team that manually monitors all open claims during the transition period — regardless of which system is tracking them — ensuring no claim breaches the 60-day deadline due to system migration issues.
2. Freeze new claims submissions to the new system until the parallel run period confirms that claims workflow is functioning correctly. During the parallel period, process claims in both systems and verify the results are consistent.

questions.stem:
A Nigerian life insurer has recently launched a bancassurance partnership with a tier-1 bank. The bank’s internet banking platform needs to allow customers to apply for the insurer’s term life product and pay premiums digitally.
(a) Explain what API integration means in this context and describe the data flows that must be supported between the bank’s system and the insurer’s PAS.
(b) Identify three NDPA 2023 compliance obligations that the API integration agreement between the bank and insurer must address.
(c) Describe the NIIRA 2025 regulatory requirements (premium receipt, agent licensing, commission) that the PAS integration must enforce for each policy sold through the bancassurance channel.
(d) Explain the premium reconciliation challenge created by digital premium payments through the bank’s platform and describe the daily process the insurer’s PAS should run to manage it.

model.h: Part (a) — API Integration: Meaning and Data Flows

API (Application Programming Interface) integration in this context means that the bank's internet banking system and the insurer's PAS are connected through a defined technical interface that allows them to exchange data in real time, automatically, without human intervention.

The customer journey and data flows:
1. Product quotation (Bank → Insurer PAS): The bank's internet banking platform calls the insurer's GET /quote API, sending: the customer's age, gender, desired sum assured, and policy term. The insurer's PAS responds with: the applicable annual premium; any applicable exclusions; and a quote reference number. This happens in under 2 seconds.

2. Policy application submission (Bank → Insurer PAS): The customer completes the application form in the bank's internet banking portal. The bank's system calls the insurer's POST /policy API, sending: full customer personal data (name, DOB, BVN, address); medical declaration answers; chosen premium; chosen beneficiary details. The PAS validates the data, runs AML screening (BVN verification; sanctions list check), and responds with: policy number; policy commencement date; first premium amount; and a policy certificate PDF.

3. Premium payment processing (Bank → Insurer PAS → Bank): When the customer pays the annual premium through the bank's direct debit or transfer system, the bank generates a payment file. The insurer's PAS receives the payment file via a POST /payment API call, applies the payment to the correct policy, and returns a payment confirmation. Any unmatched payments are flagged for investigation.

4. Policy status and self-service (Bank ← Insurer PAS): The customer can check their policy status, upcoming premium dates, and claim history through the bank's internet banking portal — the bank calls GET /policy/{id} and displays the returned data within its own interface.
Part (b) — Three NDPA 2023 Compliance Obligations

1. Data Processing Agreement (DPA): The API integration agreement must include a Data Processing Agreement specifying: the categories of personal data exchanged (name, BVN, health declaration data, payment data); the purpose of each data exchange (underwriting; premium collection; claims processing); the security standards each party must maintain; data retention periods; and the data subjects' rights (access, correction, deletion). Under NDPA 2023, the bank (as a data controller collecting the customer's data) and the insurer (as a co-controller using it for underwriting) must both be parties to the DPA.

2. Cross-entity data sharing consent: Before the bank shares the customer's data with the insurer's PAS via API, the customer must have provided explicit, specific, informed, and unambiguous consent to their personal data (especially the health declaration data, which is special category data) being shared with the named insurance company for insurance underwriting purposes. This consent must be separate from the bank's general terms and conditions.

3. Data security standards for API transactions: The API connection must be secured with: TLS 1.2 or higher encryption for all data in transit; API key authentication (preventing unauthorised parties from accessing the insurer's PAS); rate limiting (preventing data extraction attacks); and a complete data access log for every API call — enabling both the bank and the insurer to demonstrate to the NDPC, on request, what data was exchanged and when.
Part (c) — NIIRA 2025 PAS Integration Requirements

Premium receipt enforcement: The insurer's PAS must record the bank as a corporate agent for premium collection purposes. The no-premium-no-cover principle requires the PAS to activate the policy only upon confirmed receipt of the premium — not upon application acceptance. The API integration must send a payment confirmation to the PAS before the policy status is set to 'In Force.' Any policy for which the first premium has not been received must remain in a 'Pending' status until payment is confirmed.

Agent licensing enforcement: The bank staff who sell the term life product through the internet banking system must hold the CIIN Cert. COP (for staff who advise customers) or the bank must be registered as a corporate agent. The PAS must record the selling agent (or corporate agent entity) against every policy issued through the bancassurance channel — and must validate that the recorded agent has a current, valid NAICOM agent licence before commission is processed. If the agent licence has expired or been revoked, the PAS must flag the policy for compliance review before commission payment.

Commission enforcement: The PAS must calculate commission strictly in accordance with the NAICOM-approved commission schedule filed with the product approval. Commission rates above the NAICOM maximum must be flagged and blocked by the PAS — the system should not permit manual overrides of commission rates above the prescribed ceiling.
Part (d) — Premium Reconciliation Challenge and Daily PAS Process

The reconciliation challenge: Digital premium payments through the bank's internet banking system arrive at the insurer's bank account as individual transfers or as aggregated bulk transfers — not necessarily with the policy number as the payment reference. A customer paying their term life premium via direct transfer may use their name and amount as the reference, not their policy number. This creates 'unmatched receipts' — payments credited to the insurer's account that cannot be automatically matched to a specific policy.

Daily PAS reconciliation process:
Step 1 (Morning): The insurer's premium collection bank produces a daily transaction file of all credits to the premium collection account overnight. The PAS receives this file via automated data transfer by 8:00 AM.

Step 2 (9:00 AM — automated): The PAS attempts automated matching for each receipt against: the bank's API payment confirmation (the bank may send a payment confirmation with the policy number if the API integration is correctly configured); the billing schedule for that day's due premiums.

Step 3 (9:00 AM — 12:00 PM — manual resolution): Unmatched receipts are displayed on the reconciliation officer's dashboard. The officer investigates each unmatched receipt — searching by amount, bank account, and expected payment date to identify the policyholder. Matched items are confirmed; unresolved items are escalated.

Step 4 (End of day): All matched premiums are applied to the relevant policy records, updating their premium payment status. Policies whose premium was due today and has not been received are moved to 'Grace Period' status, triggering the automated conservation workflow.

questions.stem:
A life insurer’s NAICOM market conduct inspection has identified the following PAS-related findings:
(i) the claims module does not track the 60-day settlement deadline;
(ii) the agent module does not check CIIN Cert. COP licence validity before processing commission;
(iii) there is no data access log for health data accessed by underwriting staff; and (iv) the premium reconciliation is run weekly rather than daily, resulting in a 5-day lag in identifying unmatched premiums. For each finding:
(a) Identify the specific NIIRA 2025 or NDPA 2023 provision being breached.
(b) Describe the PAS configuration change required to remediate the finding.
(c) Estimate the operational risk created by the current gap while the remediation is being implemented.

model.h: Finding (i) — Claims Module: No 60-Day Deadline Tracking

Provision breached: NIIRA 2025 (s.210) — the 60-day settlement timeline from notification (the 5-day acknowledgement is the insurer’s own service standard).

PAS configuration change required: Configure the claims workflow module to: (1) automatically timestamp every claim registration with the claim receipt date; (2) calculate the 5-day acknowledgement deadline and generate an automated task for the claims officer; (3) begin the 60-day settlement countdown from the notification date, and record the 'complete documentation received' date as an internal milestone; (4) generate amber alerts at day 55 (5 days before breach) and red escalation alerts at day 59 (1 day before breach) to the claims team supervisor and Head of Claims.

Operational risk during remediation: Every day that the claims module cannot track the 60-day deadline, there is an unquantifiable risk that one or more claims will breach the statutory timeline without detection. A breach results in: compound interest on the outstanding claim for each month of delay and NAICOM administrative sanctions; the defaulting insurer being named in NAICOM's public enforcement register; and potential civil liability to the claimant. Given that this is an active NAICOM inspection finding, the regulator will specifically monitor claims settlement timelines during the remediation period — making a compliance breach particularly consequential.
Finding (ii) — Agent Module: No CIIN Cert. COP Validation Before Commission

Provision breached: NIIRA 2025 agent licensing requirements — all individuals selling insurance products must hold a current, valid CIIN Cert. COP. Processing commission to an unlicensed agent implies the insurer is aware of and enabling unlicensed insurance distribution.

PAS configuration change required: Integrate the agent module with the CIIN's agent licence registry (via API, or via a regularly updated data file if the API is not yet available). Before processing any commission payment, the PAS must: (1) look up the agent's licence status in the CIIN registry; (2) confirm the licence is current and not expired or revoked; (3) if the licence is expired or revoked, flag the commission payment as 'Blocked — licence invalid' and route to the compliance team for review before any payment is made.

Operational risk during remediation: Commission may be paid to agents whose licences have expired — making those agents unlicensed sellers in receipt of commission for policies they were not authorised to sell. The insurer faces NAICOM sanction for enabling unlicensed distribution; the policies sold by expired-licence agents may be challenged as sold through an unauthorised distribution mechanism.
Finding (iii) — No Data Access Log for Health Data

Provision breached: NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 — data controllers processing special category data (health data used in underwriting) must maintain an access log recording: who accessed the data; when; from which system or terminal; and the purpose of access. The absence of an access log means the insurer cannot demonstrate compliance with the NDPA 2023 requirement to protect health data from unauthorised access.

PAS configuration change required: Enable the PAS's audit logging module for all health data fields (medical declaration answers, HIV test results, medical examination reports, GP records). The log must capture: username of the accessing staff member; timestamp; specific policy record accessed; and the action performed (view, edit, download). The log must be: immutable (cannot be altered by the user who generated the entry); retained for the period specified in the NDPA data retention policy (at minimum the policy term plus 5 years); and accessible to the NDPC on request.

Operational risk during remediation: Without an access log, the insurer cannot respond to a data subject access request seeking information about who has accessed their health data. It also cannot investigate a data breach (it cannot determine which records were accessed, by whom, if unauthorised access occurs). During the remediation period, the insurer is exposed to: NDPC regulatory penalty for the access log absence; reputational damage if a health data breach occurs and cannot be investigated.
Finding (iv) — Weekly Premium Reconciliation with 5-Day Lag

Provision breached: This breaches the principle of NIIRA 2025's no-premium-no-cover rule — the insurer cannot accurately determine which policies are in force and which are lapsed/in grace period without daily premium reconciliation. The 5-day lag means policyholders who have lapsed may be treated as in force (creating claims liability for uncovered periods) and policyholders who have paid may be treated as lapsed (creating incorrect grace period letters and conservation outreach).

PAS configuration change required: Reconfigure the premium reconciliation to run as an automated daily batch process, preferably overnight with results available by 8:00 AM each business day. The process should: automatically import the bank's daily transaction file; perform automated matching against the billing schedule; produce an unmatched items report for manual resolution; and update all policy premium payment statuses before the business day begins.

Operational risk during remediation: During the 5-day lag period, a policyholder who has lapsed may die and the family may present a death claim — but the insurer's records (not yet updated due to the weekly reconciliation lag) may still show the policy as in force. The insurer would then need to investigate whether the premium had been paid before the death — a potentially disputed claims process that could have been avoided by daily reconciliation.

questions.stem: A leading Nigerian life insurer’s Board has been presented with two technology investment proposals: (A) Replace the existing 15-year-old on-premise PAS with a modern cloud-based platform (estimated cost: ₦850 million over 3 years, implementation timeline 18 months, full IFRS 17 and NIIRA 2025 compliance at go-live); or (B) Augment the existing system with a data middleware layer and a cloud-based digital portal while retaining the legacy PAS as the core system of record (estimated cost: ₦220 million over 2 years, implementation timeline 9 months, IFRS 17 compliance requires further work). Critically evaluate the two options from the perspective of the Board’s fiduciary duty to policyholders and shareholders, analysing: total cost of ownership over a 5-year horizon; regulatory compliance risk; operational risk during implementation; strategic flexibility for digital channel expansion; and the insurer’s position relative to Insurtech competitors. Make and justify a recommendation.

model.h: Thesis

Option A (full replacement) is the correct long-term decision and the stronger fiduciary choice — despite its higher cost, longer timeline, and implementation risk. The fundamental problem with Option B is that it preserves the exact infrastructure whose inadequacy is the source of the insurer's technology constraints. A digital portal over a 15-year-old, API-deficient, vendor-unsupported PAS is a façade — it makes the front end look modern while the foundational system remains incapable of the regulatory, actuarial, and digital capabilities the insurer needs.
Total Cost of Ownership Over 5 Years

Option A — Full replacement:
• Years 1–3: ₦850m implementation cost.
• Year 4–5: Estimated ₦100–₦150m annual operating cost for a cloud PAS (licensing, support, minor enhancements) = ₦200–₦300m.
• 5-year TCO: ₦1,050–₦1,150m.
• Excluded cost: No further legacy PAS maintenance required; no separate data warehouse for IFRS 17 (built into the new PAS).

Option B — Augmentation:
• Years 1–2: ₦220m middleware and portal investment.
• Ongoing legacy PAS maintenance (the vendor has stopped active support but the insurer must retain system administrators and likely pay for any critical patches): estimated ₦50m per year = ₦150m over years 1–3.
• IFRS 17 compliance 'further work': A separate IFRS 17 data layer will require ₦200–₦400m additional investment — deferred but not avoided.
• 5-year TCO: ₦220m + ₦250m legacy maintenance + ₦300m IFRS 17 work = ₦770–₦970m — apparently competitive with Option A, but this does not include the ongoing middleware operating cost and the API limitations that remain.

Conclusion: The 5-year TCO gap between the two options is smaller than the headline cost difference suggests — and Option A provides significantly more capability for a similar total investment.
Regulatory Compliance Risk

Option A: Full IFRS 17 and NIIRA 2025 compliance at go-live in month 18. After go-live, the insurer produces regulatory returns directly from the PAS, generates IFRS 17 cohort data without workarounds, and tracks claims SLA compliance automatically. Regulatory risk is concentrated in the 18-month implementation period.

Option B: The middleware layer may resolve the NAICOM quarterly return production delay — but IFRS 17 compliance 'requires further work.' This further work is not optional: IFRS 17 is a mandatory reporting standard for the insurer's financial statements. Option B defers rather than resolves a regulatory compliance gap — and the deferred cost and risk remain.

Conclusion: Option A provides regulatory certainty; Option B carries ongoing IFRS 17 compliance risk.
Operational Risk During Implementation

Option A carries higher implementation risk: an 18-month full replacement of the system of record for 85,000+ policies is a complex programme that can go wrong. Data migration failure, parallel run discrepancies, or vendor delivery delay could result in: operational disruption; regulatory filing delays; or the insurer being forced to extend the parallel run period and incur additional cost.

Option B carries lower immediate implementation risk (9-month timeline; no data migration required). However, it creates a different operational risk: the middleware layer adds complexity to the technology architecture — every data flow must pass through an additional layer, creating additional points of potential failure.

Conclusion: Option A's implementation risk is real but manageable with proper governance. Option B's operational simplicity is an advantage — but one that is outweighed by the long-term constraints it preserves.
Strategic Flexibility and Insurtech Positioning

Option A: A cloud PAS with API-first architecture enables: real-time embedded insurance partnerships; direct integration with any digital distribution partner; a self-service portal that reads from the live PAS (not from a middleware layer); and all future digital capabilities without additional integration work.

Option B: API integration remains constrained by the legacy PAS's API limitations — the middleware layer translates API calls, but is constrained by what the legacy PAS can expose. Any embedded insurance partnership requires middleware configuration, not direct API access.

Conclusion: Option A creates strategic flexibility; Option B constrains it.
Recommendation

The Board should approve Option A — full PAS replacement — with the following conditions:
1. Phased payment: Structure the ₦850m over 3 years with milestone-based payment — reducing financial risk if the implementation timeline slips.
2. Parallel run non-negotiable: The parallel run must run for a minimum of 3 months before the legacy system is decommissioned.
3. Independent technology governance: Appoint an independent technology project board to provide quarterly oversight of the implementation — including Board-level reporting on progress, risks, and budget variance.
4. Data migration audit: Commission an independent data audit before migration begins, and validate 5% of migrated records before go-live.

The Board's fiduciary duty to policyholders requires that the insurer's operational infrastructure is capable of meeting its regulatory obligations. Option B defers this obligation; Option A fulfils it.

questions.stem: ‘The Policy Administration System is the most important technology investment a life insurer makes, yet it is consistently the most neglected. Nigerian life insurers routinely invest in CRM platforms, digital marketing tools, and mobile apps — visible, customer-facing technology — while continuing to operate PAS platforms that cannot produce the regulatory reports required by NIIRA 2025, cannot generate IFRS 17-compliant data without manual workarounds, and cannot support the real-time API integrations that digital distribution requires. This technology debt is not just an operational inconvenience: it is a governance failure, a regulatory risk, and a strategic constraint that limits the insurer’s ability to compete in the market that digital insurance is creating.’ Critically evaluate this proposition, drawing on the specific operational, regulatory, and strategic consequences of PAS inadequacy described in this chapter.

model.h: Thesis

The proposition is accurate and identifies a fundamental misalignment in Nigerian life insurers' technology investment priorities. The PAS is analogous to a building's foundation: it is invisible to occupants (policyholders, agents, regulators) who see only the finished rooms (the agent app, the WhatsApp bot, the claims portal). But the quality of the foundation determines what can be built above it. An insurer that invests in beautiful rooms on a cracked foundation is creating a problem that becomes more expensive and disruptive to fix with every additional storey added.
Why PAS is the Most Important Technology Investment

Every other technology system the insurer operates — the CRM, the digital portal, the bancassurance API, the analytics platform — either reads from or writes to the PAS. The PAS is the system of record: the authoritative source of truth about what the insurer owes to whom, under which terms, for how much premium, with which agent commission. If the PAS data is incomplete, incorrect, or inaccessible:
• The CRM is showing customer data that may not match the policy record.
• The digital portal is displaying policy information that may be out of date.
• The analytics platform is drawing insights from a dataset that may have errors.
• The bancassurance API is issuing policies that may not be correctly reflected in the system of record.

No amount of investment in visible, customer-facing technology resolves the foundational problem of an inadequate PAS.
The PAS Neglect Problem: Why It Happens

The reason PAS neglect is rational (from a narrow management perspective) is that PAS inadequacy is largely invisible until it produces a catastrophic failure:

1. The CEO who approves a CRM investment receives a visible ROI — agents are happier, customer data is better organised, the Board can see the system in operation. The CEO who approves a PAS replacement receives: 18 months of implementation risk; operational disruption during the parallel run; a year-end IFRS 17 report that looks the same as before (but is now generated automatically rather than manually). The visibility-to-cost ratio is poor.

2. The marketing director who budgets for a WhatsApp Business API deployment can demonstrate new business leads in 30 days. The technology director who proposes a PAS replacement cannot demonstrate ROI in 30 days — the returns accrue over 5–10 years through reduced manual effort, regulatory compliance, and digital distribution capability.

3. Boards that are not technically literate will naturally approve investments whose value they can see and understand — and defer investments in infrastructure they cannot evaluate. Governing the PAS decision requires either actuarial/technology expertise on the Board or a Chief Risk Officer who can translate the PAS risk into fiduciary language.
PAS Inadequacy as a Governance Failure

A Board that allows the PAS to become so outdated that it cannot:
• Produce NAICOM quarterly returns without 3 days of manual extraction;
• Generate IFRS 17-compliant cohort data without a separate data warehouse;
• Support real-time API integration for digital distribution;
• Track the insurer’s 5-day acknowledgement standard and NIIRA 2025’s 60-day claims settlement deadline automatically —

...has failed in its fiduciary duty to ensure the insurer has the operational infrastructure to meet its regulatory obligations. This is not a management oversight — it is a Board governance failure.

The Statutory Actuary who certifies reserves and the Audit Committee that approves the financial statements both depend on PAS data quality. A compromised PAS creates a chain of dependency that ultimately means: the solvency ratio may be miscalculated; the IFRS 17 profit may be misstated; the coverage ratio may be incorrectly computed.
PAS Inadequacy as a Strategic Constraint

NIIRA 2025's embedded insurance mandate and the Insurtech ecosystem's growth create a market in which the insurer without a modern PAS is simply unable to compete:

1. Cannot participate in embedded insurance: A real-time API is required. A PAS with no API capability cannot respond to a policy issuance request in 3 seconds — the financial partner will move to an insurer whose PAS can.

2. Cannot scale bancassurance: A bancassurance partner issuing 500 policies per day cannot process them manually if the insurer's PAS has no API. The partnership collapses or remains at minimal volume.

3. Cannot compete for digital-first consumers: The consumer who applies for insurance through a mobile app expects an instant policy certificate. An insurer whose PAS takes 24–48 hours to issue will lose this consumer to a competitor whose PAS can issue in 5 minutes.

Conclusion: The proposition is not merely analytically correct — it identifies the most consequential investment decision Nigerian life insurers face. The PAS is the technology strategy. Everything else is downstream of whether this foundation is sound.
